title: Signalling & Train Control Systems (ATP / ATO / ATS, ETCS, CBTC)

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of railway signalling?
options: To guarantee safe separation between trains and give authority to move
questions.explain: Signalling keeps trains safely apart, sets routes and gives the authority to move.

questions.q: The design principle of signalling, under which any failure must result in the most restrictive and safest state, is called:
questions.explain: Fail-safe means a failure pushes the system to its safest state, not the fastest.

questions.q: In fixed block working, the line is divided into blocks and:
options: Trains may follow each other freely in a block
Only one train is allowed in a block at a time
questions.explain: Fixed block = one train per block; that space separation is the safety guarantee.

questions.q: In moving block working, the safe distance between trains is:
options: Decided by the driver by sight
Computed continuously from the preceding train's exact position
questions.explain: Moving block uses the exact, continuously updated position of the train ahead, giving shorter headway and higher capacity.

questions.q: Moving block working is the basis of which concepts?
options: Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) and European Train Control System (ETCS) Level 3 concepts
questions.explain: Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) and European Train Control System (ETCS) L3 ideas rest on moving block — continuous position, continuous safe distance.

questions.q: Interlocking in signalling ensures that:
options: All signals always show green together
Points can move under a moving train
Two trains can share one route safely
Points, signals and track occupancy are locked together so conflicting routes can never be set
questions.explain: Interlocking locks points, signals and occupancy together so two trains can never be routed into collision.

questions.q: Before a signal or authority can clear over a set of points, what must be proved?
options: The points are correctly set and locked, proved by detection
The driver has sounded the horn
questions.explain: Point detection proves the points are set and locked before any authority is given over them.

questions.q: A track circuit detects train presence in a section by using:
questions.explain: A track circuit uses the rails themselves as an electrical circuit to detect a train.

questions.q: An axle counter detects train presence by:
options: Counting wheels (axles) in and out of a section
questions.explain: Equal axles in and out means the section is clear; axle counters are used widely in metros.

questions.q: ATP stands for:
questions.explain: Protection = the safety layer that enforces speed and movement authority.

questions.q: The job of Automatic Train Protection (ATP) is to:
options: Manage the timetable at Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Enforce safety — speed limits, movement authority and braking
questions.explain: Automatic Train Protection (ATP) supervises speed against the authority and brakes the train automatically on violation.

questions.q: ATO stands for:
questions.explain: Operation = driving the train: traction, braking and accurate station stopping.

questions.q: The job of Automatic Train Operation (ATO) is to:
options: Drive the train — traction, braking and station stops
questions.explain: Automatic Train Operation (ATO) drives under the limits set by Automatic Train Protection (ATP); it never overrides protection.

questions.q: Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) stands for:
questions.explain: Supervision = managing the service: timetable, regulation and display at Operations Control Centre (OCC).

questions.q: The job of Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) is to:
options: Manage the service — timetable, train regulation and display at Operations Control Centre (OCC)
questions.explain: Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) is the controllers' decision-support layer for running the service to timetable.

questions.q: Which of the Automatic Train Protection (ATP)/Automatic Train Operation (ATO)/Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) trio is safety-critical and fail-safe?
questions.explain: Automatic Train Protection (ATP) is safety-critical and fail-safe and cannot be overridden casually; Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) is non-vital decision support.

questions.q: If Automatic Train Protection (ATP) fails, what is the effect on the service?
options: The train brakes to a stop — service stops safely
The driver continues at full speed
Automatic Train Operation (ATO) takes over safety
Trains run on sight at line speed
questions.explain: Automatic Train Protection (ATP) failure = brakes to stop. Safety first, service second.

questions.q: If Automatic Train Operation (ATO) fails but Automatic Train Protection (ATP) is healthy, the train:
options: Can be driven manually by the driver under ATP protection
questions.explain: Automatic Train Operation (ATO) only drives; with Automatic Train Protection (ATP) healthy, the driver drives manually under protection.

questions.q: If Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) fails, what happens?
options: All trains brake to a stop
questions.explain: Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) is decision support — its failure means manual regulation by controllers, not a safety stop.

questions.q: ETCS stands for:
questions.explain: European Train Control System (ETCS) is the European Train Control System, the mainline/regional standard used on Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS).

questions.q: Which signalling system does the Namo Bharat Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) use?
options: European Train Control System (ETCS) Level 2 with Hybrid Level 3 over Long Term Evolution (LTE)
questions.explain: National Capital Region Transport Corporation (NCRTC) uses European Train Control System (ETCS) L2 with Hybrid L3 features over Long Term Evolution (LTE) radio — a world-first combination.

questions.q: Movement Authority (MA) means:
options: Authority to open Platform Screen Doors (PSDs)
Permission to run to a defined point at a defined speed profile
questions.explain: The MA tells the train exactly how far it may go and at what speed profile.

questions.q: In European Train Control System (ETCS), the on-board computer continuously supervises:
options: The train's speed against its Movement Authority, braking automatically on violation
questions.explain: The on-board computer compares actual speed with the MA continuously and brakes on violation.

questions.q: In European Train Control System (ETCS) Level 1, the primary authority still comes from:
options: Continuous radio from the Radio Block Centre (RBC)
Lineside signals, with balises giving in-cab updates
questions.explain: In L1, lineside signals remain primary; Eurobalises give intermittent in-cab updates of aspect and speed.

questions.q: Eurobalises in European Train Control System (ETCS) Level 1 provide:
options: Intermittent in-cab updates of signal aspect and speed
questions.explain: Balises transmit only when the train passes over them — hence 'intermittent' transmission in L1.

questions.q: In European Train Control System (ETCS) Level 2, Movement Authority reaches the train mainly through:
options: Continuous radio from the Radio Block Centre (RBC)
questions.explain: In L2 the Radio Block Centre (RBC) sends MA by continuous radio — on Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS), over Long Term Evolution (LTE).

questions.q: In European Train Control System (ETCS) Level 2, balises are used mainly for:
questions.explain: In L2, balises only fix the train's position; authority comes by radio from the Radio Block Centre (RBC).

questions.q: In European Train Control System (ETCS) Level 2, lineside signals are:
options: Optional / not the primary means of authority
questions.explain: L2 runs without depending on lineside signals — the cab display is primary.

questions.q: European Train Control System (ETCS) Hybrid Level 3 adds capacity mainly through:
options: Train integrity proved on-board, allowing virtual sub-blocks and closer running
questions.explain: Hybrid L3 uses on-board train-integrity proof and virtual sub-blocks so trains can run closer safely.

questions.q: In European Train Control System (ETCS) L2 territory, track vacancy is still proved by:
questions.explain: In L2, track vacancy is proved by track circuits or axle counters; Hybrid L3 adds integrity-based gains.

questions.q: RBC stands for:
questions.explain: The Radio Block Centre knows each train's position and issues its movement authority by radio.

questions.q: CBTC stands for:
questions.explain: Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) is the metro-style system built on continuous communication between train and trackside.

questions.q: Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) in metros normally uses which radio medium?
questions.explain: Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) usually uses Wi-Fi-based radio; European Train Control System (ETCS) uses GSM-R/Long Term Evolution (LTE) family radio.

questions.q: European Train Control System (ETCS) on Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) uses which radio for train communication?
questions.explain: National Capital Region Transport Corporation (NCRTC)'s European Train Control System (ETCS) runs over Long Term Evolution (LTE) radio, carrying both data and voice.

questions.q: A key strength of Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) is:
options: Very short headways in metro operation
questions.explain: Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC)'s continuous communication gives metros very short headways.

questions.q: A key strength of European Train Control System (ETCS) is:
options: Interoperability across networks and countries, and suitability for high speed
questions.explain: European Train Control System (ETCS) is a cross-border standard designed for interoperable, high-speed mainline/regional running.

questions.q: Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC) and European Train Control System (ETCS) share which common features?
options: Continuous communication, precise train location, moving-block capability and Automatic Train Protection (ATP) supervision
questions.explain: Despite different radio and origin, both share continuous communication, precise location, moving block and Automatic Train Protection (ATP).

questions.q: SPAD stands for:
questions.explain: A Signal Passed At Danger (SPAD) — passing a signal at danger — is a serious safety incident signalling exists to prevent.

questions.q: Safety Integrity Level 4 (SIL-4) in signalling refers to:
options: The highest Safety Integrity Level for signalling functions
questions.explain: Safety Integrity Level 4 (SIL-4) is the top safety integrity level demanded of vital signalling functions.

questions.q: Kavach is:
options: The Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) signalling system
A type of Platform Screen Door (PSD)
Indian Railways' own indigenous Automatic Train Protection (ATP) system
questions.explain: Kavach is IR's home-grown Automatic Train Protection (ATP) — same protection idea as European Train Control System (ETCS) ATP, different system.

questions.q: In Absolute Block working, the core principle is:
options: Trains follow each other closely by sight
Only one train in a block section at a time
questions.explain: Absolute block is the oldest space-separation idea: one train, one block section.

questions.q: Automatic Block working differs from Absolute Block because:
options: It is track-circuited and signals clear automatically as trains pass
questions.explain: Automatic block uses track circuits so signals change automatically with train movement.

questions.q: Delhi Metro's train control is based on:
questions.explain: Delhi Metro uses metro-style Communications-Based Train Control (CBTC); Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) uses European Train Control System (ETCS) — the favourite examiner comparison.

questions.q: A train approaches a stop indication and the driver fails to react. In an Automatic Train Protection (ATP)-fitted Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) train, what happens?
options: ATP intervenes and brakes the train automatically
Automatic Train Operation (ATO) accelerates to clear the section
Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) informs passengers first
questions.explain: Automatic Train Protection (ATP) is connected to the brakes: violating the authority means automatic braking, unlike a road signal that only advises.

questions.q: Two trains are accidentally routed towards the same platform line. Which system is designed to make this impossible?
questions.explain: Interlocking locks points and signals together so conflicting routes can never be set.

questions.q: During peak hours, Operations Control Centre (OCC) wants trains closer together to raise capacity. Which feature mainly enables this safely?
questions.explain: Moving-block working computes safe distance continuously, allowing shorter headway without reducing safety.

questions.q: A balise failure is reported in European Train Control System (ETCS) L2 territory. What is the most likely direct effect?
options: Position reference for trains is affected; authority still comes by radio from the Radio Block Centre (RBC)
questions.explain: In L2 balises only fix position; the Radio Block Centre (RBC)'s radio authority is a separate function.

questions.q: Why is railway signalling compared to 'a traffic light connected to the brakes'?
options: Because unlike a road signal, a stop indication is enforced by automatic braking through Automatic Train Protection (ATP)
Because drivers may jump signals freely
Because signals control road traffic too
Because trains stop only by driver choice
questions.explain: A road signal advises; railway Automatic Train Protection (ATP) enforces — that enforcement is the core difference.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Automatic Train Protection (ATP)–Protection, Automatic Train Operation (ATO)–Operation, Automatic Train Supervision (ATS)–Supervision
questions.explain: Memorise: Automatic Train Protection (ATP) protects, Automatic Train Operation (ATO) operates (drives), Automatic Train Supervision (ATS) supervises (regulates).

questions.q: In European Train Control System (ETCS) Level 2 working, the train continuously reports its position to the Radio Block Centre (RBC) mainly so that the RBC can:
options: Update the movement authority for that train based on its actual position
Change the timetable for the next day
questions.explain: In European Train Control System (ETCS) L2 the train's position reports let the Radio Block Centre (RBC) keep each train's movement authority accurate and safe — this is what allows trains to run closer together safely.

questions.q: 'Overlap' in signalling is:
options: The distance two trains share on one platform
A safety margin of track kept clear beyond a stop signal, in case a train overruns it slightly
The common portion of two timetables
questions.explain: The overlap is spare room beyond the signal: if a driver brakes a little late, the train stops inside the overlap instead of reaching the danger point.

questions.q: 'Flank protection' means:
options: Guarding the sides of a station building
Protecting a set route from conflicting movements that could approach it from the side
questions.explain: Flank protection locks or guards side routes and trap points so nothing can roll or be driven into the side of a train using the protected route.

questions.q: 'Approach locking' of a route ensures that once a train is approaching on a cleared route:
options: The route cannot be altered at once; it can be released only after the train passes or a safety time delay expires
questions.explain: Approach locking stops a signaller from changing points in the face of an approaching train that may be unable to stop — a classic accident-prevention feature.

questions.q: A 'calling-on' signal, where provided, authorises a driver to:
options: Call the control room on the radio
Proceed very cautiously past a stop aspect, typically to enter an occupied line or couple to another train
questions.explain: Calling-on is a controlled exception: the driver moves at a speed at which he can stop short of any obstruction, because the line ahead may be occupied.

questions.q: The Driver Machine Interface (DMI) in an ETCS-fitted cab shows the driver mainly:
options: Current speed, permitted speed and the movement authority ahead
questions.explain: In European Train Control System (ETCS) working, the cab display — the Driver Machine Interface (DMI) — replaces lineside signals with live speed and authority information.
